awd_titl_txt: Proposal for a Workshop to Bring Together a Community of Paleontology Journals, Online Article Repositories, and Databases to Chart a FAIR Future for Their Data
awd_abstract_narration:
This workshop will bring together members of the paleontology community to determine best practices for sharing and reusing published scientific data. This workshop will provide collaborative space to generate and exchange ideas and strategies, especially in today’s rapidly changing scientific publishing and data dissemination landscape, where emerging methods are increasing the amount of data that can be harvested from scientific papers. The workshop will focus on: 1) new approaches to data gathering to support and facilitate scientific research; 2) ways to ensure that researchers who contribute paleontological data, as well as the journals that publish it, receive proper credit and are supported and recognized for their work; 3) ways to ensure that data sources can be continually verified, modified, and updated; and 4) new and innovative ways to use these data to engage with the public. Workshop participants reflect the breadth of the field and include editors of paleontology journals, developers of fossil databases, and individuals and organizations involved with sharing scientific literature, collections, data, and educational resources online.

Scientific publishing and data dissemination are changing rapidly with the development of new methods that extract high volumes of data from scientific papers. In paleontology, systematic publications contain extensive amounts of data that have not been previously culled. These systematic data are foundational to paleontology, and the publications represent invaluable repositories for several scientific disciplines. The workshop comprises plans to develop the most effective ideas and approaches to make these data resources and publications Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) and to encourage community support for this effort. This workshop will convene editors of peer-reviewed journals, contributors to online data-sharing platforms, organizations sharing systematics literature online, and practitioners in systematics, collections digitization, and education. The specific aims of the workshop are to generate and share techniques and approaches to: 1) best enable the rapid collection of paleontological data from the literature to make data more broadly available to scientists and the public; 2) better ensure that authors and venues that publish these data be properly cited and credited; 3) develop methods to continually evaluate the veracity of the underlying data; and 4) better connect authors and publishers with those building and maintaining the databases to create a mutually supportive framework.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
The project involved holding a workshop at the University of Kansas to bring together the paleontological community, editors and authors of systematic paleontology publications produced by scientific societies and natural history museums, and National Science Foundation (NSF) supported data publishers and repositories, to develop community-driven strategies for making the data they produce and share more Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reproducible (FAIR). As part of the workshop, community buy-in was obtained for such efforts, and steps were identified to ensure that individuals who collect and curate specimens, and who conduct systematic research, receive formal credit for their work even when such work is aggregated into larger databases. There were 26 individuals who participated representing: paleontologists from major natural history museums and universities; editors of systematic paleontology journals; student representatives of the Paleontological Society, along with other graduate students; and individuals from organizations supported by NSF who play an important role in making data on museum specimens as well as heritage systematic publications available.

As part of the workshop, techniques and approaches were solicited to: 1) increase the pace that paleontological data is collected from the literature, to make currently less accessible data more available and usable to scientists and the general public; 2) better ensure that authors who collected data be properly cited and credited, to incentivize future work in systematic paleontology and data generation; 3) develop a framework to help determine the accuracy of data; and 4) better connect authors and editors of systematic paleontology publications with those building and maintaining databases and data repositories.

Collaborations and connections across different areas of the paleontological community and with those sharing data online were created. A perspective on the pathways that scientific data take before and after publication and the factors influencing how data are shared was developed. An impact/effort matrix was also created to help prioritize where activities to increase the sharing and publishing of FAIR data should be directed to have the greatest benefit. A paper is being written that will share the results and findings of the workshop.

Five graduate students participated in the workshop and built connections with professional paleontologists, editors of systematic paleontology journals, and those sharing data. They also learned about how data are collected and shared as part of the publication process and how to make paleontological data more FAIR. The importance of sharing information on fossils with the general public, including images and information to aid in identification and learning, was also discussed.
